py-finally-controlflow:
A real decision was made: "A return/break/continue inside a finally block silently cancels any in-flight exception, treated as ordinary control flow with no warning (CPython behavior through 2019, re-affirmed by the Steering Council's 2019 rejection of PEP 601)."

Several real options were considered at the time:
- status-quo-linters: Keep current semantics: return/break/continue in finally silently cancel exceptions; treat this as a style issue for linters (Pylint/flake8-bugbear) and PEP 8, not a language change.
- pep601-forbid: Deprecate then forbid return/break/continue that exit a finally block: emit SyntaxWarning in 3.9/3.10, then turn it into a SyntaxError.
- change-semantics-exception-wins: Change the semantics instead of forbidding the syntax: keep return/break/continue legal inside finally, but make any in-flight exception always win (propagate) over them.

A later real incident/trigger occurred:
"Irit Katriel's empirical study of the top 8,000 PyPI packages (120,964,221 lines of code) found 203 real instances of return/break/continue in a finally block, of which 149 (73%) were incorrect and introduced unintended exception-swallowing bugs; of 40 maintainers who responded within two weeks, 35 acknowledged the problem and 15 opened a fix PR. This is the cost/benefit data PEP 601 lacked in 2019."

Given this incident, which ONE of the listed option ids does it most vindicate (i.e. which option would now get adopted instead)? Reply with ONLY the option id, nothing else.
py-script-deps-format:
A real decision was made: "Python script dependency metadata should be embedded as a simple, line-based comment block with a custom header/footer marker, not a structured data format (PEP 722's chosen design, proposed 2023-07-19)."

Several real options were considered at the time:
- comment-block: Use a plain comment block (e.g. a '# Script Dependencies:' header and footer line, one requirement per line) -- readable without a parser, no quoting rules.
- toml-block: Embed a TOML-formatted metadata block instead of a plain comment block, reusing pyproject.toml's own data format for consistency with the rest of Python packaging.
- embed-pyproject-toml: Embed an actual (partial) pyproject.toml file inside the script, reusing the existing [project] table instead of inventing any new format.

A later real incident/trigger occurred:
"The Python Steering Council's PEP delegate (Brett Cannon) rejected PEP 722 in favor of a TOML-based alternative, PEP 723 (authored by Ofek Lev, created 2023-08-04), citing consistency with pyproject.toml's existing TOML-based packaging metadata and the 'common frustration' with inconsistent formats raised in the recent Python Packaging Survey."

Given this incident, which ONE of the listed option ids does it most vindicate (i.e. which option would now get adopted instead)? Reply with ONLY the option id, nothing else.
py-subinterpreters:
A real decision was made: "True parallel execution of Python code uses multiprocessing (separate OS processes), because the GIL serializes all threads within one interpreter; CPython's C-API-only multiple-interpreters feature is not exposed to pure-Python code (status through 2023, reaffirmed by PEP 554's non-acceptance)."

Several real options were considered at the time:
- multiprocessing-only: Keep multiprocessing as the only accessible parallel-execution path; CPython's C API multiple-interpreters support stays internal/undocumented for Python-level code.
- interpreters-stdlib-module: Add a stdlib 'interpreters' module exposing subinterpreters plus a channel-based communication API directly to pure-Python code.
- pipes-based-comm-api: If a stdlib module is added at all, communicate between interpreters via raw OS pipes directly, instead of a higher-level channel/queue abstraction.

A later real incident/trigger occurred:
"PEP 703 ('Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython') was accepted and PEP 684 (a per-interpreter GIL) shipped, making genuine multi-core parallelism inside one process newly practical and renewing demand for a stdlib-level way to create and use multiple interpreters without the C API."

Given this incident, which ONE of the listed option ids does it most vindicate (i.e. which option would now get adopted instead)? Reply with ONLY the option id, nothing else.
py-lockfile-format:
A real decision was made: "No standard lock-file format exists; each tool (pip freeze, pip-tools, Poetry, PDM) defines and reads its own incompatible lock-file format (status through 2022, after PEP 665's non-acceptance)."

Several real options were considered at the time:
- status-quo-per-tool: Keep the status quo: no cross-tool standard; each tool's own lock format stays authoritative for that tool.
- standard-lockfile-format: Define one standard, tool-agnostic lock-file format so any installer can consume a lock file regardless of which tool generated it.
- adopt-poetry-lock-as-standard: Rather than invent a new format, standardize on Poetry's existing poetry.lock format, already in wide use.

A later real incident/trigger occurred:
"Continued fragmentation across 5+ incompatible lock-file formats left tooling (Dependabot, cloud dependency installers) unable to support users uniformly, and the lack of secure defaults (hash pinning is opt-in-only in most formats) left installs exposed to dependency-substitution supply-chain attacks."

Given this incident, which ONE of the listed option ids does it most vindicate (i.e. which option would now get adopted instead)? Reply with ONLY the option id, nothing else.
py-annotations-eval:
A real decision was made: "Function/class/module annotations are automatically converted to strings at compile time and left unevaluated ('stringized annotations', PEP 563's design, accepted 2017, status quo through 2022)."

Several real options were considered at the time:
- stringized-annotations: Keep annotations as compiler-generated strings (PEP 563); solves forward-reference problems for static type checkers by never evaluating annotation expressions at runtime at all.
- deferred-eval-function: Delay evaluation of annotation expressions by compiling them into a hidden per-object function (an 'implicit lambda expression') that is only called when annotations are actually requested, instead of stringizing them.
- store-strings-lazily: Keep storing annotation strings (as PEP 563 does) but make retrieval lazy/opt-in via a new accessor function, without compiling a hidden per-object function.

A later real incident/trigger occurred:
"Stringized annotations (PEP 563) caused chronic problems for runtime users of annotations (dataclasses, Pydantic, attrs, and similar libraries that read __annotations__ at runtime): they had to eval() the strings in a reconstructed namespace, which is slow, can fail on forward references to genuinely out-of-scope names, and loses non-literal annotation values."

Given this incident, which ONE of the listed option ids does it most vindicate (i.e. which option would now get adopted instead)? Reply with ONLY the option id, nothing else.
py-enum-type:
A real decision was made: "Python has no dedicated enumeration type; code represents a fixed set of named values with plain int or str module-level constants (status quo through 2013, reaffirmed by PEP 354's 2005 rejection)."

Several real options were considered at the time:
- int-constants: Keep using plain int/str constants for enumerations; add no new stdlib type.
- pep354-functional-enum: Add a functional enum(*names) constructor returning an opaque enumeration object, with no class syntax.
- flufl-style-class-enum: Add a class-based Enum type (subclass Enum, define members as class attributes), based on Barry Warsaw's flufl.enum third-party package.

A later real incident/trigger occurred:
"A new python-ideas mailing-list discussion on adding an enum type to the standard library reopened the question PEP 354 had closed in 2005, driven by continued real-world pain from magic integer constants in standard-library APIs (e.g. socket.AF_INET) that lacked friendly string representations."

Given this incident, which ONE of the listed option ids does it most vindicate (i.e. which option would now get adopted instead)? Reply with ONLY the option id, nothing else.
